title: Research Bite #74: Digital Amnesia: The Aftermath of a Screenshot
author: Craig Barton
summary: In Research Bite #74, Craig Barton summarises a seven-experiment study by Sophia P. Fabrizio, Rebecca Lurie, and Deanne L. Westerman testing whether screenshotting art images on a smartphone -- despite the well-documented memory cost of photographing rather than simply viewing -- delivers any compensating benefit predicted by cognitive offloading theory. Across 892 undergraduates, screenshotting produced a large, consistent memory cost in every experiment with almost no offsetting gains: no improvement in source memory, no boost on a subsequent demanding task, and no advantage learning material that came afterward, with only one narrow benefit surviving lenient scoring. Barton translates the findings into direct classroom guidance, warning that telling students to "just take a photo" of the board signals them not to engage with the content, and that the memory impairment persisted even though the screenshotting task in the study took only a second and required no unfamiliar equipment. He recommends that any student capture be paired with a deliberate return to the material -- rewriting it in their own words -- and suggests handwritten notes as a default alternative to photographic capture, while noting the study's limitations (US undergraduates with art images in a lab setting, untested on older adults or real lesson content).
points: Across all seven experiments and 892 undergraduates, screenshotting images produced a large, consistent memory cost with essentially none of the predicted compensating benefits from cognitive offloading -- no gain in source memory, task performance, or subsequent learning.

The memory impairment did not shrink when the capture was fast and effortless, undermining the common teacher assumption that a "quick snap" of the board is harmless because it barely interrupts the lesson.

Barton's key practical translation is that a photograph of content only pays off if students deliberately return to it and rehearse it -- capture without a planned revisit produces no learning benefit, mirroring what happens to most images left in a camera roll.

The study's "illusion of having got it" finding -- students felt material was safely stored via screenshot even though they had lost the detail -- supports using a brief phones-away retrieval check at lesson's end rather than relying on captured content as evidence of learning.

Barton explicitly flags generalisability limits: the sample was US undergraduates working with art images in a lab, not school pupils with curriculum content, and the one detected benefit was small and scoring-dependent.
quotes: Photography is one of the most common uses of a smartphone, and earlier work has shown that images we capture are remembered worse than images we simply look at. This study asked whether that cost buys us anything in return.

Screenshotting produced a large, consistent memory cost in every experiment. The predicted benefits did not appear: no better memory for where information came from, no improvement on a demanding maths task, and no boost to learning the material that came next.

But as we see in this experiment, students captured images on their own phones, in a task that took a second and involved no fiddling with unfamiliar equipment, and still remembered them substantially worse than images they only looked at.

The authors are explicit that their findings apply to material that is captured and then never revisited, which describes most of what sits in a camera roll. If students do photograph something, make the return trip part of the instruction.

Participants screenshotted material while genuinely engaged in a task about art, and still lost the detail. The feeling that something is safely stored is not a reliable signal that it has been learned.
Overall, these findings suggest that screenshotting imposes considerable memory costs without offering compensatory benefits.
